rationale: B wins because it keeps the four usable story shapes and does cleaner surgery on the evidence. A's "A nonprofit is giving an AI tutor to teachers for free while the rest of ed-tech charges per seat" spends facts it was not given. B's "Donors, not districts, are paying for the AI tutor headed to 1 million more students" is sharper, more testable, and less tempted by fake category drama.
gaps_in_A: "while the rest of ed-tech charges per seat" is not in the update. That is an invented market contrast, even if the proof section later tries to ask for competitor pricing.
"one of the largest AI-tutoring deployments" may be true, but it is not supplied. Bring comparative deployment evidence or cut it.
"landing in named districts" overreaches because no districts are named in the update. The angle knows it needs that proof, but the copy still acts as if it has it.
The teacher lesson-planning feature never gets a disciplined proof path. A notes it, then mostly lets the student-outcomes story carry the load.
gaps_in_B: "Its own study is the first test of that claim" is a little too absolute. The update says first classroom results, not first test in any broader sense.

"Donors, not districts, are paying" is directionally grounded, but the update only says free to teachers and donor-funded. B correctly asks whether districts pay, but the headline should not outrun that answer.

"The district is joining the rollout, or its pilot results are part of what is being published now" fudges two different district statuses. A pilot district and a newly added district are not automatically the same local story.
The next step should rank the proof gates: methodology first, named district second, critic/spokesperson third. The contrarian angle still needs a real skeptic before anyone pitches it.
